Understanding PET, CT and MRI scans

Scans show where something is and how big it is. They rarely tell the whole story alone. Here is what each one does, and how to read the report without panicking.

The three main scans

  • CT (computed tomography)Uses X-rays taken from many angles to make detailed cross-section pictures. Fast, widely available, and the most common scan for the chest, abdomen and pelvis. It often uses contrast dye by vein or by mouth. Tell the team about kidney problems, diabetes medicines such as metformin, or a past reaction to contrast.
  • PET or PET/CT (positron emission tomography)A small amount of a radioactive tracer — most often a sugar-like tracer called FDG — is injected. Many cancers use more sugar than normal tissue, so they “light up.” It is usually combined with a CT in the same machine. You will be asked not to eat for several hours beforehand; if you have diabetes, ask for specific instructions.
  • MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)Uses a strong magnet and radio waves, with no X-ray radiation. Especially detailed for the brain, spine, liver, pelvis and soft tissues. It is loud and takes longer. Tell the team about pacemakers, metal implants, or if you get anxious in tight spaces.

Reading the report

  • Start with the “Impression.” This is the radiologist’s summary at the end. The “Findings” section above it lists everything seen, including many normal or harmless details.
  • “Incidental” or “nonspecific” means something was seen that may not be important. Many incidental findings turn out to be harmless, but ask whether follow-up is needed.
  • “Stable” means no meaningful change from the last scan. In cancer care this is often good news.
  • PET “uptake” or “SUV” describes how brightly an area lights up. Bright areas can be cancer, but inflammation, infection, healing and normal tissues can light up too.
  • Results posted to your patient portal may appear before your doctor has reviewed them. It is fine to wait and go over them together.

Good to know

  • Always say if you might be pregnant or are breastfeeding.
  • Bring a list of past scan dates and places; comparing with older scans is often the most useful part.
  • A scan usually cannot confirm cancer by itself — a biopsy usually does. See understanding my pathology report.
